utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This afternoon we'll hear the 98 bis submissions from the parties, and we begin with the Defence for Milan Lukic, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I must admit, though, I'm kind of at a loss in terms of how to approach 98 bis, and as I've been reading the rules and the decisions on 98 bis, it seems like an almost insurmountable -- seems like an almost insurmountable rule because -- and I'm noting your decision, Your Honour, in Dragomir Milosevic in where you discuss the evolution of the rule as it was changed in 2004. And the quandary I have is, I think, in relation to the reason that the Sredoje Lukic team has elected not argue a 98 bis is because it seems like the standard has evolved to a point where so long as the Prosecution presents some evidence on each count, some evidence, then a 98 bis would not be appropriate. Now, I'm in a quandary, Your Honour, because part of me wanted to go through a dissertation, of which I would not be prepared for today, outlining the inconsistencies or cross-referencings between certain witnesses, some for alibi rebuttal but are also incorporated into the different counts. But I realised that in looking at the rulings, that would be inappropriate, because at this point in time according to 98 bis: "At the close of the Prosecution's case, the Trial Chamber shall, by oral decision and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties, enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence of supporting a conviction." Now, what does that mean, Your Honour? And I guess I challenge the Court to draw a line in this case, because this case is different. I think it's different than what this rule was written for because by this being a first party commission case, the rule, as it's written, technically shifts the burden of proof to the defendant because it limits the Court's ability to look at this case. Matter of fact, Your Honour, it reads very similar to a directed verdict motion in my jurisdiction where the Court, if there is some evidence to move beyond, then of course the Judge either says, Defence put on your case and/or it goes to the jury, because of course they are the ones that are going to be the ultimate determiners of the facts. But in your case, you technically pass it on to yourselves. And so what happens is, that, because technically under a hypothetical situation, Your Honours, we could put on no defence. We could put on none. And it's still the burden of the Prosecution to have proved every element of each crime beyond a reasonable doubt. And on the hypothetical that we would put on no defence, you would have missed an opportunity to rule it 98 bis based on counts that you believe, and it really limits the Court's ability to narrow down the case as it goes into the Defence case because, one, of course the Prosecution has showed their hand, if you will. And the way 98 bis is written today, it forces the Defence to show their hand on all counts with limitations on the Court to decide a portion, or, for instance, a bifurcation of a single count because, of course, if you look at the indictment of the case, Count 1, persecutions, may give a broad scope of conduct. And to be honest, Your Honour, for purposes of 98 bis from a factual perspective, we think Count 1 would survive anyway. But when you look at, for instance, the Drina River or Pionirska Street or Bikavac, there are five counts per alleged crime, and 98 bis as written disallows the Court for looking into each count, separating them and deciding whether or not the burden has been met at each level. So again, Your Honour, in a quandary situation, I think that Rule 98 absolutely prejudices a defendant only in so much as it has the practical effect of shifting the burden of proof to the defendant at an improper time in the case, considering that today, as it stands alone, the Prosecution should have enough on each count to convict my client beyond a reasonable doubt. And if it does not, because you are the fact finders that shift the case back on to themselves, you really have to take the time to analyse this case in a first commission case. Because I understand the differences between a joint criminal enterprise or a leadership and command responsibility wherein the evidence presented might not touch on a particular person's actions or direct actions, direct crimes, i.e., I shot you, I killed you. And so in looking at this, Your Honour, I think the rule is inadequate today and our preparation should have been more of a let's outline everything, let's show the credibility problems of the witnesses, and see if the case stands on its own two feet today. Because, Your Honour, looking at the rule, absent some minor technicalities, and not so minor, actually I take that back, but absent some technicalities, I think, factually speaking, the Prosecution has probably done close to its job in at least getting it past the requirements of 98. Now, we do need to look at the facts as is though and see if 98 bis is appropriate for some or all of the counts based on the failures of the Prosecution to lay out the fact that this was a war. And I'm not saying that there was never a war, but I'm saying was there a war in June of 1992. Because we have some facts before us. We have that fighting started and there was a skirmish between people on the dam early April, okay. We have that the Uzamnica Corps came into town, some bad things happened as a result of that but supposedly they left. Now, I've been here trying to push some of the interrelations because we are not running from the fact that Mr. Milan Lukic was a reserve police officer at the time, embroiled in this situation; however, the Prosecution has elected in their case in chief to avoid that completely. They've avoided it. As a matter of fact in their most recent submissions, they appeared to be denying it completely. They want to separate Milan Lukic from this otherwise broader power spectrum in the region. But I think that has a practical and fatal flaw. Is by divesting Mr. Milan Lukic from the conflict, they in fact divest him from the jurisdiction of the War Crimes Tribunal itself. By turning Milan Lukic into a rogue, someone that is acting without any tacit connection to the power structure involved, not under the command of Dragomir Tomic, not under the command of Risto Perisic, not under the command of Branimir Savovic, but simply a rogue as alleged in the complaint or in the -- excuse me, in the indictment, he was supposedly a paramilitary leader. A leader of a specific group called the White Eagles, and yet, the Prosecution is in some such and based -- really based on the evidence as presented, I mean, they can't control what their witnesses say, but their witnesses have said other things. Their witnesses have said that Colonel Jovanovic was in control of the White Eagles. Other witnesses and victims have said that the White Eagles were held up in the hotel. Other people have said that these White Eagles came from Serbia, yet no one really has established this relationship between Milan Lukic and this bigger sect of "White Eagles." And even that, they haven't created a nexus or a relationship between the "White Eagles" and the grander scheme of things. Because I would argue without that, the allegations as set forth in this complaint are simply domestic crimes, and notwithstanding of the earlier 11 bis proceedings, those domestic crimes should be prosecuted in the domestic jurisdiction. I don't even think these are war crimes. They would be alleged as robbery, assault, battery, all the way up to murder. Absolutely. But by saying that this is part of the War Crimes Tribunal, no one has really established when the war started. No one has really brought this in, and if you want to take the limitations of the Court in terms of Mr. Masovic, I think that intensifies the problem. It intensifies it from a legal factual perspective, because unless we have that -- because I mean, Your Honour, I guess I speak from my heart, I speak what I believe and even if I'm wrong you'll know that I've really wrestled with this. And I wonder why in a region so plagued by crime, so plagued by tragedy with so many victims, the end all be all of the Bikavac conflict area -- or, excuse me, the Visegrad conflict area is a former bartender, a former police officer, and a now convicted waiter. No apparent ties to the leadership, by the OTP's presentation. To be honest, I would like to see more of a leadership -- because I think the War Crimes Tribunal in and of itself was meant for that. To create a court that transcends sovereignty, that transcends ordinary courts, that transcends and has the power to bring and haul in people from anywhere in the world, it's meant for the architects. It's meant for the architects, Your Honour, because what the architects that did -- that was so dastardly, that was so horrendous, is they changed the rules for an entire population by playing and manipulating old hatreds, old prejudices. They did this through in-advance propaganda, waging terrible allegations against a people. These allegations were acted upon by ordinary citizens who lacked the sophistication, the education, or the introspection to stand alone in a time period when standing alone in and of itself could be dangerous. In denying that Mr. Lukic is a part of this power structure or this chain of command that can in fact arrest people and disappear people and persecute people, round up women, put them in a hotel for horrible things, then they must have laid a case that what put Mr. Milan Lukic, a former bartender, in that position. Because I don't think that any -- by any stretch of the imagination from what has been presented in this courtroom over the last few months can really put Milan Lukic as a leader. At best, he was a leader of a small clique of friends. And as far as the witnesses have been able to tie him, those small group of friends were associated by the most simple of relationships, i.e., blood, or kum relationship. So this is not a relationship born of loyalty to a party or an ideology, or anything else. At most, a lot of the actions described are opportunistic crimes that were created, and those opportunisms were created by a grander scheme, a bigger political structure that Milan Lukic had no ability to influence, correct or change the course. And that's important because before we raise the jurisdiction of this place, of this Court, of the United Nations, of the planet that are willing to right a wrong, if you are going to go after a waiter and a bartender, and a police officer, you had better show evidence of the grand scheme. Because other than that, they are just alleged criminals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say first that there's no evidence of a war, of an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that is a prerequisite for the commission of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes. And I would -- and I would argue that -- I mean, I have such a hard time, because I know people were dying, of course, people were fighting. But when did it transcend this level of a disorganised civil discourse that was really was precipitated from outside. There were -- I mean, I think we've all been around here long enough to know that the big forces involved were manipulating a large, relatively ignorant population. People that, Your Honour, were existing in an economic crisis. You want to talk about the customs and standards of war? I think we could create a prediction model for this kind of tragedy that's almost mathematical because I think any time a nation state has been allowed by the international community to descend into such terrible poverty, I mean, we heard in this courtroom 50 billion Dinars bought your life. It's my understanding that 7.000 Dinars was a penny. And so what does that transcend to, to be a dollar? And so if you want to look at any time tragedy has been allowed to work its way in, it has been in the poorest and the most ignored regions of our planet. Nazi Germany elected Hitler in the worst economic times and the world community allowed the German people, following World War I, as punishment to descend in this economic problem that then precipitated a tyrant rising in their midst, democratically elected to a certain degree. So what do we have, what is it the tangential relationship between the Bosnian conflict and the Rwandan conflict, or the Sudanese conflict, is that the international community allows a set of people to get so desperate that any powder-keg event can cause an absolute de-evolution of our civilisation for a time. I would argue that another thing that the OTP has failed to prove in this case as a prima facie prerequisite is that the acts or conducts of my client, as alleged, could be -- and I guess the words are right out of the indictment, that the persecutions of the Bosnian-Muslims and other non-Serb civilians on political, racial or religious grounds. Well, we may have a greater understanding -- we may have a greater understanding of the motivations of that architect sect, but I don't think that we've really entered the mind or the motivations of this bartender or waiter or police officer. There has been evidence before the Court that Milan Lukic had many Muslim friends. There has been evidence before the Court that he never caused trouble in high school with Muslims, never fought them, never had this discourse. But what we have heard though, is, is that Milan Lukic is from Rujiste. And Your Honour, Rujiste is at the end of the road right next to Slap, which you have heard about. Slap is that bend in the river where the bodies were collected by Mr. -- I think it was a protected witness, but they were buried there but that was also considered the "frontlines." So what did Milan Lukic do and what is the evidence that's been presented for the Court but that Milan Lukic was in Switzerland, he didn't even live there, and he came back to the region only after whatever conflict we can define it as started. Again, Your Honour, with no evidence that this is anything more than him returning to his home country in a time where I think we can argue that anyone in the region would be in some kind of danger, especially people living near the "frontline." It's arguable that Milan Lukic like many young men in that area at the outset were forcibly mobilised, drafted. You participate or you are an outsider. There's been evidence that in fact, and it's in dispute of course, it's in dispute by me but it was presented by the Prosecution, that Milan Lukic killed Serbs. And so if you want to argue the fact that it is a prerequisite that the persecution or the acts be based on a religious or ethnic racial grounds, then I argue that they've presented absolutely no evidence of that fact. I think one of the problems with the case that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How would you find that evidence? Isn't it by way of inference from the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you. I can see how you can see that because the inference is so powerful in my mind because I watch the news and read the -- you know, like everybody else, but the fact is, is I think in a direct commission case, it really goes to the motives of the actor. By inference, you could argue that but aren't you arguing transferred inference. Transferred intent. This isn't a JCE so we got to look into the mind of Milan Lukic whether we like it or not. And if you add to this fact, Your Honour, that Mitar Vasiljevic, we know broke his leg the day of the fateful fire in Pionirska, and I take absolutely different positions with Pionirska as Bikavac, I think the presentation of the Defence and where we've gone with that takes a different position. But in Pionirska, regardless of that fact, I think the Court has to entertain the fact that assuming Mitar Vasiljevic hurt himself at 5.00 and was no longer able to participate in either Bikavac or Pionirska, and the second amended complaint is notably devoid of Mitar's name, but that does not eliminate the fact that several groups of witnesses especially related to Bikavac but including Pionirska, are adamant and absolutely unwavering in their assertion that Mitar Vasiljevic participated in the late night situation at Pionirska, as well as Bikavac, and things in between. I think that is a real problem because one of the things that despite leaving the name out in the second amended indictment or maybe not asking questions on direct, or because the statements were in such a way, but under 92 ter you've seen all these statements, you've seen all these conflicting statements that have come in. And one of the things, though, that was noticeable is that these witnesses were not ready to let go of Mitar. They just weren't. And the interesting thing that how ID now comes into this is because in the Mitar Vasiljevic case, most of these witnesses, pre-trial, outside the courtroom, were given lineups and they successfully ID'd Mitar. Now, it's arguable that those same people put Mitar at the Bikavac location on June 27th, and so that just means they were familiar enough with him over the years to pick him out of a picture, but otherwise lying or grossly mistaken about his presence. And if they can be grossly mistaken about his presence and so much so that their statement almost puts him arm and arm with Milan, I recognise them together because. And you've -- ID is a huge issue because you've watched these witnesses struggle with ID. In the courtroom they have struggled, and that to me is beyond comprehension because the courtroom ID is the most suggestive process on the planet given this setup, given the uniforms we have to wear. In fact, every witness that sits there, they don't have to have seen a picture of them, they don't have to have watched the news, they don't have to do anything. All they have to know are the two names, I assume they did that, they all gave statements, and they have to know who is older. If you know who is older, a hundred per cent of the time given ordinary human common sense, those people would get an in-court ID correct. And yet there's been problems. That problem does go into the witness statements themselves when the alibi rebuttals -- I mean, it was just unimaginable to me that I come and the alibi rebuttals for a crime are a new crime. A serious crime. Not -- not, you know, I saw him shoplifting at the store that day, that's why I know he was in town. No, it was, He raped me this day. He killed my friend this day. That's powerful. But you got to look at them for a second. One of those alibi rape victims said he had tattoos on his arm. I would have expected him to have tattoos on his arms. One of them says he had blond hair blue eyes. I would have expected that. So there's a real problem with ID issues that goes into Pionirska, and I think just like the Court separated Mitar Vasiljevic at Pionirska, there is an issue of -- I think the Court needs to be open the possibility, let's just call it a hypothetical, that I can be there robbing you in the afternoon, but it doesn't necessarily mean I'm part of the group that's killing you at midnight. Think about that for a second. Because if you think of Pionirska by itself, there was two mother and sons survivors and a couple of other people, the young girl, the young girls, the sisters, as well as the old gentleman. And those are all the survivors. Well, the interesting thing about the mothers was, is that they saw -- one, they are married to who was there at the beginning and married to Mitar Vasiljevic being there. At the end of the night in the dark when the lights are out and there's only flashlights and there's no power, who is there? They see these guys. Well, we all know Mitar couldn't be there; he in the ambulance getting a shot of alcohol with his ambulance driver on his way to the hospital. Okay. So what happens then? The older women only count the three or four. I think that's really powerful because, one, they are mistaken because Mitar is not there; and two, what do their sons see? What do the younger girls see? The sons see a column of soldiers down to Pionirska. Several. The girls saw a roadblock at the end of the street, a blockade. We cannot eliminate the possibility that there were much more people involved, by no means were they run or commanded by Milan Lukic, and that in fact, it was that maybe grander power structure that had it out for those people. The one exception that I do have with Pionirska as a theory is that it was not a fire in the traditional sense. Why, because the picture shown by the Prosecution didn't have all the carbonisation that we would expect. You look at the floor boards in that photograph and they are burnt but there has been a little fire in the middle, almost like teenagers went and drank their beers there, hanging out. There's clearly small arms fire and weapons impact in the walls. The survivors of Pionirska heard screams and gun-fire for 30 minutes to an hour. That is not evidence of people being burned up because the fire would consume and kill them. That was evidence of survivors of what, a grenade attack? Shrapnel wounded the mother that exited the room and there was a grenade? Who is to say that these soldiers didn't simply attack them with grenades and guns, and didn't try to burn anyone alive in the house. It was the impression of the survivors that led to that conclusion. Not necessarily that that was a factual situation. But I think we need to be open to the fact that the OTP failed entirely to prove the presence of my client at that fateful point in time. Not vis-a-vis alibis or anything else, but simply because their evidence didn't rise to that level and they never ever, ever, ever dealt with Mitar being injured. They didn't deal with that. They didn't put it to their witnesses, Hey, look, you might have been mistaken, are you sure? No. They came in here sure of Mitar. And that is a problem because, Your Honours, if 92 bis -- excuse me, Rule 98 is appropriate, then you should never ever look at the facts of the case and say, You know what, if the Defence doesn't put on a case today, has the Prosecution met beyond a reasonable doubt today? That's really the possibility. And I would argue that, by virtue of their time constraints and everything else, at best what was put on here was a summarized version of what I think should be a much more in-depth and detailed presentation of the facts. And maybe those facts are incorporated in all those statements we admitted, but on the same token, I expected more details. And the number one person I expected those more details from, Your Honour, was Ms. Turjacanin involving her being in that fire. If you look at her statements, if you look at her transcripts of the news interviews and if you look at her testimony in court, her memories of that fateful moment of when she was taken from her home, put in a fire supposedly and escaped never escapes a paragraph with not all the requisite details and feelings and emotions other than you would expect but without all the details that I would expect in a court of law. Problematic points of the case on two focal points. One of which is, both Pionirska and Bikavac, there has been insufficient documentation or evidence of the deaths. Bikavac, in the complaint, listed 16 people associated with it. Pionirska, 70. If you believe Ms. Turjacanin, 70 people were in that house. Forensics has been done, no human remains have been found. This is a home that supposedly collapsed in on itself, presumably breaking, shattering or otherwise entombing 70 people's charred and brutalised remains? And yet not a single tooth, bone shard, finger bone, fingernail, skull fragment, anything, was presented from that site. We saw pictures, it looks like it's a ruined foundation where some people have thrown their trash, but no real evidence, and basically we are all left to suppose where the remains of the house went. We can imagine the worst of possibilities. But the problem is, is the Prosecution did not present any evidence to that fact. So we have a single potential eyewitness victim who -- Your Honour, I believe Ms. Turjacanin was brutalised. I don't necessarily believe it was by the fire. I believe she was attacked in that neighbourhood. The reason being, Your Honour, is right from their own witnesses, the alibi witnesses, remember all these women that are in the Bikavac neighbourhood that meet Zehra and she tells their story and they believe her. Remember every single supporting witness in Bikavac talked to Zehra. A couple of them claim to have seen skulls and bones poking out of ruins, but yet they all spoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say you believe she was attacked. Attacked by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I believe she was a victim of the rape scenario that was going on in the area. The reason being, Your Honour, is rape victims in and of itself all state how they were trapped there, could not leave, and otherwise didn't have a method of egress, waiting for convoys or whatever promises were meant. These women were being taken out and returned at different intervals and they all describe this. I find it hard to believe. And this is an environment where Ms. Turjacanin's own brother was walled up in their home right under their very noses. This is a situation where a number of women were taken and returned for their mothers not to ask question but everyone knew something horrible happened to them. I found it hard to believe that Zehra would have spent two weeks as a young lady in this neighbourhood and not been a victim of this back and forth transport of women that was evidenced by those other ladies. So if you think about that for a second, it is the perfect impetus for the trauma to be transferred on something else. I ask yourself, Your Honour, is -- is -- even other witnesses for the Prosecution had heard Ms. Turjacanin had burned herself on a stove. I ask yourself to look at her -- think of her injuries, Your Honour, and her description of the fire. She burned herself on a door that was too hot to touch. Well, that doesn't explain the burns on the back of your arms. That's explained by being immersed in some fire. I submit that her first description of her injuries to doctors and Serbs that she caught herself on fire is -- and her injuries are consistent with the household accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But she gave an explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: She did. I would expect her to. And that's been -- what is tough, Your Honour, is, you know, part of me wants to acquiesce to your wishes to put things straight on to a witness, but yet on the same token, sometimes I want to marry a witness to their statement because when you compare against someone else's or some other bit of evidence, that's when it becomes silly. I can't do that with every person nor do I want to shatter Ms. Turjacanin's belief system. I think that's dangerous. I think it's dangerous that no one has taken care of her in all this time and gotten her psychological help. She claims to have only seen a psychologist for 30 minutes, and yet this is a woman that now speaks another language because of the trauma she experienced in that area. And I can't even begin to address that. But I think the reasonable possibility exists she was injured, that she was traumatized that she was victimized, but the Bikavac in itself did not happen that way. The simplest, most logical way I believe that, Your Honour, is her own brother in his statement stating that she had never met Milan Lukic with him. That goes a long way. A lot of these witnesses in their IDs claim to have seen him on the bus, gone to school with him, but if that were all true, Milan would have to be older. He would just have to be older. I mean, we all know, I think it's judicial notice of his birthday at this point, and too many people came across this courtroom and said they knew him; but when pressed for the details of why, when and how they had that knowledge and familiarity, they failed. They failed here on the stand to explain why and how they knew him. And when queried about age differences and things like that that would be ordinary, they digress to I know him, he is from Rujiste and a repetitive discourse of sticking to stories that no longer made sense. I would argue that the killings of seven men at the Varda factory are from a perspective of witnesses that did not have the requisite vantage point to make such identification. The reason I say that, Your Honour, is that the Prosecution relies way too heavily on the allegations of the taking of Behija's Passat. The reason think it's overreaching is that in at least three statements that I have looked at, just kind of trying to get a sense of the case again last night, three people ID'd him in different cars. Three people. And not to say that the Passat wasn't an issue in that town. Of course it was. I can't deny that. But I think it's just as logical as that it could have been used by a multitude of people in a time when every Muslim car was technically being robbed from the populace and given to the authorities. The Muslim property was turned into the carpool of the SDS and the establishment. They rely way too heavily on people at a distance where they would be absolutely disadvantaged to actually identify a single person that they did not know extremely well or have some kind of magnifying device to assist them. If you even look at the Drina River incident, Your Honour, the gentleman VG-79 across the river had binoculars. So much so he could clearly identify victims by name because he knew them. And even in that particular case, he saw only three gentlemen all in black with skulls on their heads and a Peglica instead of a Passat, and a Yugo, which I think at that point became undisputed. And so although I would agree that I think the Drina River, given Mitar's testimony at length in the previous trial, makes that the most difficult one to say couldn't survive a directed verdict motion or a 98 motion or anything related to it, still there are problems on identification. There are problems because the gentleman even the two victims believe was Milan Lukic had his face painted. And one of them clearly remembered a large mole near his mouth. This case is such that certain aspects of it for the Prosecution have fallen apart. And it is under the jurisprudence of this Court that almost falling apart is required to get past Rule 98. And I would argue to a certain degree certain aspects of the case have fallen apart. The Koric murder. A single witness. Will it make it past? I think the ID is still an issue for that single witness that testified. There was a single statement in contradiction to that that was not admitted yet. So I don't think it's as relevant to this point, but I think it's a very weak case given the nature of the identity and the limited witnesses that participated in that. And like I said, Your Honour, I believe Pionirska in itself could be divided. The beatings at the Uzamnica camp, from a Rule 98 perspective we would concede there's probably enough there, but it's interesting how the first statements and even on direct -- excuse me, on cross-examination a couple of the witnesses came back to only seeing Milan Lukic there three or four times, but yet after their testifying, it was almost every day. And you got to wonder, well, why did it -- I think to convict Mr. Lukic, you wouldn't need every day. You really only need three or four times if that was the threshold, but it was interesting from a motivated witness standpoint how the first statements could evolve from a few to, like I said, every day. If you are not going to look at the credibility of the witnesses, at this point, you know, maybe that's just a moot point, but I think it's something to consider for purposes of looking at that which I believe is a pretty serious count. Again we have not been able to present the evidence for some of that time in the Uzamnica allegations. Mr. Lukic was in fact in jail and I think that brings some problems. But again, that probably wouldn't preclude a Rule 98 defeat. So all in all, Your Honour, I'd ask to you bifurcate Pionirska. I'd like you to rule in our favour for a 98 against the actual fire and deaths allegations considering the adjudicated fact of Mitar Vasiljevic and the ID issues that have been presented in the court in the witness statements, because ID is a number one issue here. I'd ask you to dismiss Bikavac in its entirety. And understanding that the Drina River and Uzamnica and the overall persecutions could withstand at least the strict construction of the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you identify the counts specifically that you are asking us to dismiss.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In relation to -- I'm conceding enough under the ordinary Count 1, persecutions. In looking at Counts 2, 3, and 4, and 5, that relates to the Drina River, although I believe there's problems, I think from a Rule 98 perspective, these would survive under an ordinary analysis. Looking at Counts 6 and 7, we would ask you to dismiss the Varda based on problems. And I must say, that the problems of identification for our co-accused help the overall picture for a 98 perspective, because I think some of the identification issues for Mr. Sredoje Lukic are even more difficult or even more egregious. People that said they should have known him no longer saw him and I think that goes to the overall credibility problem of the ID case in this matter. Looking at the Pionirska Street, I would ask to you bifurcate simply based on the adjudicated fact and the, again, problems with identification. We would ask you to bifurcate out and dismiss Count 8. Count 9, Count 10 and Count 11, inhumane acts, I think can transcend deaths or murders, and cruel treatment, that can be alleged as anything earlier in the day beyond the actions of the evening. However -- and in Bikavac which is Counts 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17, we would ask that they be dismissed in their entirety. The killing of Ms. Koric, Counts 18 and 19, we would ask that they be dismissed in their entirety. And Counts 20 and 21, we would concede would not meet the muster of 98 bis under its current writing. And the entire indictment should be dismissed if the Court were to find a failure of the Prosecution to meet its burden into proving an armed conflict existed that was part of a widespread and systematic application based on the prejudicial motives of race, ethnicity and religion. I don't believe they've met their burden. And other than that, Your Honour, Mr. Lukic has to fight a case in Serbia where he has already been sentenced to 20 years and I think he should be allowed to go fight that case. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The applicable standard of proof for a 98 bis decision is that the Court must grant the motion wherever a reasonable trier of fact could not base a conviction on the evidence presented. Conversely, it must be denied where there is sufficient evidence upon which a Trial Chamber could enter a conviction. Of critical importance to this standard is that the Trial Chamber could convict and not that it would convict. A Chamber's decision at this stage does not bind it in its judgement. The standard for a judgement of acquittal under 98 bis is well settled. In the Dragomir Milosevic case, Your Honour Judge Robinson expounded on the applicable standard as follows: "Significantly, the test proceeds on the basis that the Prosecution case is accepted, and therefore ... at this stage, the Trial Chamber is not concerned about contradictions or inconsistencies in the Prosecution's case, or, more generally, with issues of credibility. Those are matters to be addressed by the Trial Chamber in determining the guilt of the accused at the end of the case." What remains unclear to me, however, Your Honours, is the effect of Sredoje Lukic's waiver of his right to make submissions under Rule 98 bis. There is an interpretation of the rule that the Chamber is still obliged to assess the evidence related to each accused. It is, therefore, my intention to briefly summarize the relevant evidence indicating Sredoje Lukic's culpability as well as Mr. Milan Lukic's culpability unless directed to do otherwise by the Chamber. Before I begin my review of the evidence, I would like to make a few preliminary remarks. The first has to do with transcript references. It is my intention to avoid unnecessarily citing transcript references to the evidence I will discuss. I have prepared my remarks in such a way as I will in most cases be able to refer the Chamber to a precise transcript reference if called upon to do so. In the event the Chamber would like to know a transcript reference for anything I say, please interrupt me and I will be happy to oblige. The second preliminary matter I would like to address is the use of in-court identifications of the accused. The parties have filed lengthy submissions on the law related to in-court identifications. In preparing for this submission and having reviewed the evidence carefully, I believe that the Prosecution can comfortably meet the standard of 98 bis without relying on in-court identifications. Given that our view of the jurisprudence places upon the Chamber an obligation to engage in a detailed analysis of a witness's prior knowledge and familiarity with an accused before relying on an in-court identification, it may be more expeditious to avoid reliance on them at this stage unless necessary. I will therefore not refer to any in-court identifications as, again, I believe the standard of 98 bis is clearly met without them. Should the Chamber disagree with respect to any count and come to the belief that the Prosecution can only meet its burden under 98 bis through reliance on an in-court identification, I would of course ask the Chamber to give me the opportunity to address that particular issue with respect to specific counts and specific witnesses. It is the Prosecution's position that in each of the charged crimes there is at least one recognition witness as defined by the relevant jurisprudence and upon whose in-court identification the Chamber could rely. The first crime alleged in the indictment occurred at the Drina River on the 7th of June, 1992. The Prosecution's evidence with respect to the Drina River incident charged in Counts 2 through 5 of the indictment exceeds the requirements of Rule 98 bis. The Prosecution's four key witnesses for this incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cepic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour, but could Mr. Groome speak a little bit slower because it is quite difficult for interpreters to translate in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome you heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution's four key witnesses for this incident paint a picture of these events that is both clear and consistent. The Chamber will recall that these witnesses include the two survivors of this execution, a man who watched the execution from the opposite bank of the Drina River, and other evidence taken in closed session. The story that emerges from these witnesses' testimony is the following: In the afternoon of the 7th of June, 1992, Milan Lukic and a group of other soldiers captured VG-014 and VG-032, as well as five other men in the houses where they were staying in the Bikavac neighbourhood of Visegrad. Milan Lukic forced VG-014, VG-032, and the other prisoners into two cars, one of which was the red Passat that had previously belonged to Behija Zukic. The Chamber has heard ample evidence about her death and Milan Lukic's subsequent use of her car and his arrest in October 1992 in possession of that car. Milan and the other soldiers then drove the prisoners to the Vilina Vlas Hotel. After a short time at the hotel, they were driven to a junction known as the Sase junction. Near that junction, the cars were parked and the prisoners were forced out and marched down to the Drina. They were forced to face the river, and the soldiers behind them began shooting at them. Five of them were killed. VG-014 VG-032 were not hit and managed to play dead and, thereby, survive. The evidence related to the identification of Milan Lukic as the perpetrator of this crime is as follows: VG-014, who was born in the same year as Milan Lukic and attended school with him for two years, testified that he recognised Milan Lukic instantly when he came into VG-014's house and that he had no doubt about that recognition. VG-032 had also seen Milan Lukic before the day of the Drina River incident. He had first seen Milan Lukic at a cafe where other people identified Milan Lukic to VG-032. He next saw Milan Lukic after Behija Zukic's murder, when Milan Lukic arrived at the Visegrad Health Centre where VG-032 worked, driving Behija's red Passat. VG-032 had a good opportunity to observe Milan Lukic on this occasion as Milan Lukic got out of the red Passat. He recognised him as being the same person who had been previously identified to him at the cafe. VG-014 and VG-032 also give nearly identical descriptions of Milan Lukic on the day of the Drina River incidents. Both observed a bandage on the inside of his elbow. The Chamber now has before it the protocol book from the hospital in evidence as P165, and in that book an entry for the 7th of June indicates that a person by the name of Milan Lukic received an injection. Your Honour, I'd ask if we could now move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To summarize, the Prosecution's evidence with respect to the Drina River incident is capable of supporting a conviction on these charges and exceeds the requirements of 98 bis. Counts 6 and 7 of the indictment charge Milan Lukic with murder as a crime against humanity and murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war for the killing of seven workers from the Varda furniture factory on the banks of the Drina River. The indictment charges that these killings happened on or around the 10th of June, 1992. The Prosecution led evidence from three witness with respect to this event; VG-017, VG-042 and VG-024. Each of these witnesses saw the incident from a different perspective, and each tells a different part of the overall story. VG-042 watched these events from the terrace of her house which was about 50 metres from the sawmill gate and about 100 metres from the place where Milan Lukic killed the men by the side of the river. She testified that from that distance she was able to recognise the victims and Milan Lukic. VG-017 was watching from a hiding place behind some barrels and in a henhouse. VG-024 was at work inside the factory where she was able to observe the events from a short distance, even having the opportunity to speak with one of the victims. On the morning of the day in question, VG-017 and VG-042 saw the red Passat arrive near the guard house at the sawmill gate at the Varda furniture factory. VG-017 and 042 saw three people getting out of the car, including Milan Lukic. After Milan Lukic got out of the car, he went into the workshop and brought a man by the name of Nedzad Bektas down to the guard house. He then returned to the factory floor and brought out other workers. VG-024 testified that about half past 11.00 on that day, a man named Mirko Dukanovic told her to go behind the factory because it was almost noon. VG-024 briefly left the factory with her colleagues Naza and Hajra but returned after a few minutes because she wanted to see what was going on. When she returned to the factory she saw Milan Lukic coming out of the polish section of the factory bringing Hamed Osmanagic, Nusret Aljusevic, Sabahudin Velagic and Lutvo Tabakovic with him. And on his way out he picked up Ibrisim Memisevic. He didn't take these men out the main gate; rather, he took them towards the sawmill. When Milan Lukic came out of the sawmill with the workers, he re-entered the field of view of the VG-017 and VG-042. VG-017 said that he brought out six or seven workers. 42 testified that Milan Lukic then forced the prisoners to walk down to the Drina River in one group "like sheep." VG-17 indicates that the men were taken down to the river in two groups. The first group composed of three persons, the second group of three or four. VG-042 testified when the men reached the bank of the river, Milan Lukic made them line up one next to the other and killed them one by one. He then fired another burst of gun-fire into the bodies. After killing the men at the river, Milan Lukic began walking back. He saw VG-042 and the others watching on the terrace and shot a burst of gun-fire at them. He then got back into the red Passat he had arrived in and drove back towards town. I'd ask that we go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to her great familiarity with Milan Lukic, Witness VG-024 also had a chance to closely observe him shortly before the Varda factory killings. VG-024 testified that Milan Lukic was "almost a regular visitor" to the factory, an employer of many from the factory -- an employer of many from the Muslim community. Milan Lukic would just come and just walk through the factory sometimes, she testified. VG-024 also testified about one particular occasion a few weeks before the charged incident when Milan Lukic took away several Muslim co-workers of hers. In addition, she testified that Milan Lukic identified himself as "Milan" to one of her co-workers, and was addressed by another co-worker, as "Milan." Under these circumstances, there can be no reasonable doubt about VG-024's be ability to identify Milan Lukic on the day of the Varda factory killings. VG-042 also had a solid basis for her recognition of Milan Lukic. VG-042 testified that she knew Milan Lukic when he was a boy. Like VG-024, she knows that he went to primary school first in Klasnik, and then in Prelovo. She would regularly take a bus to a co-op; this was the same bus that Milan Lukic would take to school. VG-042 testified that she took this bus trip countless times and that she did see a great deal of Milan Lukic during this time. VG-042 also testified that Milan Lukic is from Rujiste and that her family had fields near his family's fields. VG-042 knew Milan Lukic's mother Kata and his father Mile. She said Milan Lukic's parents were on good terms with her parents. They would greet each other and occasionally drink coffee or brandy together. VG-042 described how she also would exchange greetings with Milan Lukic's parents. In addition to this familiarity with Milan Lukic, his family, and his upbringing, VG-042 also had an opportunity to see Milan Lukic immediately before the incident in which the seven Varda factory workers were killed beside the Drina. VG-042 testified that earlier that same day, Milan Lukic had come to the Varda sawmill with his Passat and parked at the gate. Milan Lukic got out of the Passat and gathered up three workers: Ramiz Karaman, Ahmed Kasapovic, and VG-042's husband. He put them all into the Passat and drove them off towards the town. VG-042 testified that as they drove towards the town, they went right in front of her house. VG-042 thus had a strong fundamental familiarity with Milan Lukic as well as an opportunity to observe him immediately before the killing of the seven men by the Drina. She thus provides a strong and reliable identification of Milan Lukic that strongly corroborates the evidence of VG-024. While VG-017 was not as familiar with Milan Lukic as VG-024 or VG-042, he had seen him multiple times before the killings at the Varda factory and had a solid basis for recognizing him. VG-017 testified that he had seen Milan Lukic two or three times before the day that Milan Lukic came and killed the seven workers by the river. In addition to this occasion, VG-017 testified generally that he saw Milan Lukic when the war began, when Milan Lukic started going around VG-017's neighbourhood when the killings started. VG-017 also testified that Milan Lukic used to pass by his house all the time in the car that he drove to the Varda factory on the day of the killings. He testified that on the day of the killings, he got a look at Milan Lukic's face. When asked how he could recognise Milan Lukic here in court, he answered: "How wouldn't I? I know him. I know the man." Taking the evidence of these three witnesses together, it is clear that a reasonable trier of fact could convict Milan Lukic of the killings at the Varda factory charged in Count 6 and 7 of the indictment. Koritnik is a town in the municipality of Visegrad and is located approximately 7 kilometres from the town itself. After several weeks of increasing harassment and attacks against the village, on the 13th of June, 1992, a local Serb told the Muslim residents of Koritnik they had to leave the following day. On Sunday, the 14th of June, 1992, the Koritnik group left. Approximately 50 Bosnian-Muslims, including elderly men, women, children, and a two-day-old baby comprised the group. All members of the Koritnik group hailed from the same family, the Kurspahic family. None of them was armed, none of them wore military uniform. After a long trip on foot, the Koritnik group arrived in Visegrad around noon. Once there, Serb soldiers in front of the police station screamed at the group that they should go to the Red Cross. The Red Cross office was closed, so the group moved to the new hotel or the Visegrad hotel. Mitar Vasiljevic arrived and directed the group to the Mahala settlement in which Pionirska Street is located. Many of the Koritnik group knew this neighbourhood because they had relatives who lived there. The column of about 70 people made its way to Pionirska Street. The majority of the Koritnik group began entering the house of Jusuf Memic. Around seven others entered the house of Jusuf's son, Mujo Memic, but later joined the larger group in Jusuf Memic's house. Mitar Vasiljevic arrived. He addressed the group. He told them that buses would be provided the next day to take them to Kladanj. He presented one of the Koritnik group, Mujo Halilovic, with a piece of paper, instructing the group to present it as a document of guarantee for their safety. He told the group to stay together. Ultimately around 70 people crammed into the Memic house. Around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m., four men arrived. Roughly half an hour after Mitar Vasiljevic departed. Soldiers kicked open the door and Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, Milan Susnjar, and other armed men entered. None of these men wore anything to cover their faces. One of the men introduced himself as Milan Lukic. VG-101 immediately recognised Milan Lukic, having gone to school with him where she saw him every day. After she finished secondary school, she continued to see him at social events. Her sister, VG-078, also knew Milan Lukic from school. They attended the same school in Prelovo for seven years. VG-078 identified Milan Lukic when he entered from where she stood about metre and a half away from him. The men had stormed in, and in the rush of events, VG-101 recognised Milan Lukic first and then spoke to her sister VG-078. It was at that time that VG-078 was able to put a name to her former schoolmate's face. VG-084 corroborated Milan Lukic's identification, testifying that a quarter of the people in the room knew him and that "there were girls in the house who used to go to school with him, so they used to be school mates." A cursory examination of the list of victims attached to the indictment bears out that a number of victims were of similar age and quite likely in school with him. VG-018 stated that Sredoje Lukic also introduced himself. VG-038 knew Sredoje as a police officer in Visegrad, and used to see him on his way to school. For seven years while he went to primary school in Visegrad, he saw him as frequently as every other day excluding weekends. Additionally, Sredoje Lukic was a colleague of VG-038's relative, Huso Kurspahic. VG-038 knew Sredoje Lukic from seeing him often in his relative's company. VG-013 testified that she saw Sredoje Lukic often at social gatherings and that they had grown up in neighbouring villages. VG-013 also knew him in his official capacity as a police officer, and her father-in-law knew him. She was present with her father-in-law when Sredoje Lukic used to come by and testified that her father-in-law would offer him coffee. Also highly relevant to the issue of identification is the instantaneous recognition by a large number of people in the group. These people who perished that night knew both the accused well and their statements are now before the Chamber. I will make more detailed submissions regarding the weight that should be placed on these but would simply note at this juncture that even in common law jurisdictions which adhere to rigorous rules regarding hearsay would admit and place significant evidential weight on these statements as exceptions to the general hearsay rule. These witnesses or victims had no time nor motive to fabricate. They spontaneously uttered the name to the persons they saw at Pionirska Street. Several of these victims were close in age to Milan Lukic, and it is reasonable to conclude that from their statements that they knew him from school. Witnesses or victims such as Ramiza Kurspahic. Huso Kurspahic was told by his father Hasib, who survived the fire, that Ramiza Kurspahic told him that she went to school with Milan Lukic. Sajma Kurspahic, approximately 20 years of age, she told VG-048 that she knew Milan Lukic from school. Ismeta Kurspahic, approximately 26 years of age the night of the fire, she told VG-013 that her husband sat at the same bench in school as Milan Lukic. Other young women such as Jasmina Vila, Dzheva Kurspahic, Izeta Kurspahic, Latifa Kurspahic, and Medina Kurspahic were all close in age to Milan Lukic and it is reasonable to infer that they attended school in Visegrad along with him. Others like Jasmina Vila had been previously victimized by Milan Lukic. Similarly, the Chamber must take into account Ifeta Kurspahic who was 17 at the time and taken from the house by Milan Lukic. Both of those women, upon their return, identified Milan Lukic as the person who had taken them from the house and returned them. Finally, VG-013 described how Kada Sehic, approximately 39 years of age at the time, identified Milan Lukic by name to her as the person who took away her son and her husband. The Koritnik group surrendered all of their possessions to Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic and their men, and were subsequently subjected to a humiliating strip search before the group left. The men promised that they would be back. Around 10.00 in the night, the noise of a loud car broke the tense silence. A vehicle arrived and shone its headlights into the house. Milan Lukic approached the Memic house and knocked on the door. He was carrying a rifle. Sredoje Lukic accompanied Milan Lukic. Milan Lukic, positioned at the doorway of Memic house, ordered the Koritnik group to move to a different house, telling them that the Memic house was not safe for them. As VG-013 passed the doorway, she was less than 30 centimetres away from Milan Lukic. Edhem Kurspahic, one of the others in the Koritnik group, said that Sredoje Lukic was walking alongside the column as it made its way to the Omeragic house. One of the group directed the Koritnik group -- one of the armed men directed the Koritnik group to the Omeragic house. He ordered the group to walk another member who held a handheld torch light and lit the group's way toward himself. Admittedly the sun had already set by this time, but witnesses have recalled for the Chamber lighting from a number of sources in addition to these handheld flashlights. From the car itself, from the light outside the Memic house, from the light outside the house across from the Memic house, and from lights from the housing development behind the Omeragic house. There was sufficient light for the witnesses to see the men who led them to the Omeragic house and ultimately set them ablaze. VG-078 identified Milan Lukic throughout the move between the Memic house and the Omeragic house. She managed to escape and saw Milan Lukic walk between the houses from a distance of about 30 steps. VG-038 identified Sredoje Lukic and Milan Lukic, and the other men as transferring the Koritnik group to the Omeragic house. Also, VG-101 identifies Milan Lukic as standing in front of the Omeragic house in a lit area. Inside the Omeragic house, the Koritnik group occupied the lower floor. About 70 women, children and elderly men were crammed into the two-windowed apartment. VG-013 describe the carpets as being stained with a sort of liquid that stuck to their feet and it exuded a smell. The only door to the room in which the Koritnik group were put was closed. After a short time, Milan Lukic threw some sort of device, something like a bomb at the door. As the witness described, flames appeared as large as the door itself and reached up to the ceiling. When the door was opened, the fire was immediate and blazing. VG-101 and VG-078, who had managed to escape during the transfer towards the Omeragic house, could now hear shooting from the house next to the creek. A few of those barricaded into the house were able to escape. VG-018 and her son VG-084 were able to get out through one of the windows. Similarly, VG-013 and her son VG-038 were also able to escape out the window. Hasib Kurspahic, who had been the last person to enter the room in which the Koritnik group was held, ran out of the door when it opened. He jumped into the creek and laid down in cover for the shooting. He would tell his son shortly thereafter that Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic had been directly responsible. The evidence of the witnesses who watched the fire and heard sounds of the victims dying, the fact that they have never seen their family members again contradict Mr. Alarid's assertion that there was never a fire there. 71 human beings died in the house burning at Pionirska Street. In support of the annex A of the indictment, the following individuals are named. Prosecution Exhibit P39 contains a list of these victims as affirmed by the witness Huso Kurspahic. Your Honour, before I move into the Bikavac portion of the submission, would it be convenient to take the break there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to raise two matters for your consideration. First, in my view, you are not required to make submissions in relation to Mr. Cepic's client, Sredoje Lukic. No submissions were made on his behalf in respect of 98 bis. I know that the rule is perhaps silent on it, but it does say after hearing the oral submissions of the parties, and if a party has made no submissions, then I can't see the need to address it. At rock bottom, the procedure we have here is still adversarial and a party system. I don't rule out the possibility that the Chamber could proprio motu, in an appropriate case itself raise 98 bis, if a party doesn't. For example, if it is evident on the evidence that a legal ingredient is missing from a crime, and a party doesn't raise it, I think the Chamber would have an obligation to do so. But generally, I would say that where a party does not intend, and has made it clear, to apply 98 bis, there is no need to -- for the Prosecutor to answer. The second point I wanted to make is that Mr. Alarid made what I think is an arguable case in relation to the presence of an armed conflict. That is, of course, one of the chapeau requirements of the crimes that are charged and I'd like to you consider it. What I understand him to be saying is that the violence in the area did not reach a level where it could be characterized as an armed conflict. It was sporadic. And he even went further to say that it was just criminal activity. It wasn't a matter for the consideration of this Tribunal. I believe that's a worthy submission that requires your attention. We'll take the break now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, Counts 13 through 17 of the indictment charge Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic with extermination, murder and inhumane acts as crimes against humanity, and murder and cruel treatment as violations of the laws and customs of war with regard to the burning of a house in Bikavac settlement of Visegrad on or about the 27th of June, 1992, in which approximately 70 civilians were killed and one civilian who survived was badly burned. The Prosecution led evidence from four witnesses regarding this incident: VG-035, VG-115, 119, and the sole survivor, Zehra Turjacanin. Each of these witnesses testified about these events from a slightly different perspective. VG-035 saw Milan and Sredoje Lukic immediately before they went off to commit the crime. VG-119 saw them both immediately before and immediately after, and saw Zehra Turjacanin afterwards, in her grievously injured state. VG-115 watched the crimes being committed from her place of hiding in a nearby orchard. And finally, Zehra Turjacanin was inside Meho Aljic's house and survived the fire itself. Despite the fact that each of these women experienced these events from a different perspective, their collective testimony tells a remarkably consistent and coherent story, one which, in the Prosecution's submission, would clearly allow a reasonable trier of fact to convict Milan and Sredoje Lukic for this crime. The first witness to see Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic in the Bikavac neighbourhood on that day was VG-035. Milan Lukic had already been to her house twice that day, and Sredoje Lukic had already been there once. VG-035 testified that both Milan and Sredoje Lukic returned to her house between 4.00 and 5.00 in the afternoon of the 27th of June. They brought one other soldier with them, one whom VG-035 did not know. Milan and Sredoje Lukic took all of VG-035's money and jewellery, and then Sredoje Lukic left. Milan Lukic stayed for awhile longer and then left as well. When Milan Lukic left, VG-035 saw that he had a car with him and recognised it as Behija Zukic's car. There was loud music coming from the car, which VG-035 could hear inside her home. The car drove a short distance and parked. VG-035 was still able to hear the music coming from the car. Some time after Milan Lukic left, VG-035 heard loud shooting, a lot of shrieking and screaming. VG-119 was the second witness to see Milan and Sredoje Lukic in the Bikavac settlement on that evening. At around 8.00 p.m., someone began knocking on the door of the house that VG-119 was staying in. When the door was opened, a group of Serbs entered the house. VG-119 recognised Milan Lukic among them. When the men arrived, VG-119 could hear music playing from the cars outside. The men who came into the house asked if there were any women from the Zupa area of Visegrad in the house. When the residents told them that there were not, the soldiers left, saying that they would return. Altogether, they had remained in that house for 10 to 15 minutes. When the soldiers left, the women in the house where VG-119 were staying, could still hear the loud music coming from the cars. Zehra Turjacanin, the survivor of the fire, was the third witness to see Milan and Sredoje Lukic in Bikavac that evening. Ms. Turjacanin testified that she also remembers that the 27th of June, 1992, was the Orthodox holiday of Vidovdan. On that day, Ms. Turjacanin was at home with a group of family members and neighbours. At some point during the day she went across the street to visit her neighbour. She remembers it was evening when she left that neighbour's house. When she arrived home, she went out on her balcony to smoke a cigarette. And from that balcony, she heard very loud Serbian nationalistic music coming from the loud speakers of some car below. Shortly after she heard the music, someone began knocking on her door. When the people in Zehra Turjacanin's house opened the door in response to the knocking, a group of soldiers and other men ordered them out of the house. Ms. Turjacanin, her family, and neighbours who were gathered in the house left it with the exception of her brother Dzevad and her cousin who were hiding in the house. When she went outside, Ms. Turjacanin was told they would leave on a convoy to Bajina Basta, but she could see no buses or other vehicles capable of transporting them to safety. Ms. Turjacanin specifically remembers that Milan Lukic was one of the soldiers in the group. Milan Lukic was standing on the path separating Ms. Turjacanin's old house from her new house when she saw him. VG-119 testified that both she and Zehra Turjacanin, after the fire, eventually ended up in Medjedja. There, VG-119 would go visit Zehra every day. One day, journalists interviewed Ms. Turjacanin and asked her who was responsible for her injuries. VG-119 heard Zehra mention the names of both Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic. After having left their houses, Ms. Turjacanin and the other residents of the surrounding houses followed this group of armed men for approximately 100 metres to another house. This house belonged to Meho Aljic. Ms. Turjacanin testified that at the moment she entered the house, she saw a large group of people sitting against the walls of the room she was in, which was a combined living-room and kitchen. Ms. Turjacanin stayed close to the glass door through which she entered. Her sister Aida was right next to her. The other people in the house with Ms. Turjacanin were mainly young mothers with small children. There were also a few elderly women and men. The youngest child in the house was about a year old. Ms. Turjacanin testified that an atmosphere of fear gripped that room that she and the others were imprisoned in. After they entered, the armed men who had put them in the house began throwing rocks at the house to break the windows. Then they threw in several grenades. After the grenades exploded, a fire broke out in the room that spread very quickly. Ms. Turjacanin's clothes caught fire. Ms. Turjacanin decided to try to escape through the glass door through which she had entered. When she got to the door, though, she found that the way was blocked by a metal garage door that had been placed up against the glass door. The garage door had some small openings in it. Ms. Turjacanin was able to climb through one of these openings and escape, though her hands were badly burned within she touched the hot door. When she escaped from the house, Ms. Turjacanin saw the men who had set the fire lying in the grass about 100 metres away. The men saw her as well and yelled for her to stop. She ran, and as she was running, she took off her burning clothes. She ran towards the Serb neighbourhood of Megdan. Your Honours, I ask that we briefly move into private session.
