utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-035 also saw evidence of the fire. At around 9.00 p.m., her mother-in-law told her to go look at something through the bathroom window of the house. She went and looked and saw a huge flame. She testified that she had never seen a flame so high and assumed that a house must be engulfed. VG-119, who had seen Milan and Sredoje Lukic in her house earlier that evening, also saw Milan Lukic after the fire. According to her evidence, at about 10:00 p.m., the same group of soldiers had come into her house earlier that night had returned. This group included Milan Lukic. The lights the were on in the house, and VG-119 could see that the soldiers were dirty and dripping with sweat. Ms. Turjacanin testified that after escaping from the burning house, she was severely burned on her face and hands and felt very ill. Nevertheless, she returned to Bikavac to warn the remaining residents to leave. Ms. Turjacanin testified that she went to four houses in Bikavac to warn the residents. The fourth house she visited was the Salic family house. VG-119's testimony confirms this account. VG-035 also saw Zehra Turjacanin after the fire. She estimates that Zehra arrived at her house after midnight. When VG-035's mother-in-law opened the door, Zehra told them that Milan Lukic had set everything on fire and that she had tried to save her sister but wasn't able to. Ms. Turjacanin then left saying that she was going to warn others. Following Zehra's warning, VG-035, her children and her sister-in-law tried to flee Bikavac. They passed by the house and smelled burned bodies and burned hair. In the end, they were unable to leave that night. Each of the witnesses who testified about these events had a good opportunity to observe Milan Lukic on the day in question. They were each familiar with Milan Lukic from before, and thus, had a solid basis for recognizing him. On the night in question, Ms. Turjacanin had an excellent opportunity to observe Milan Lukic. She also had a solid basis for recognizing him. She specifically recalled seeing Milan Lukic two times in the minutes preceding the inferno at the Meho Aljic house. First, she saw him standing near her house, when she and her family first came out of their house. Second, she saw him when he took her gold chain from her neck as she was entering Meho Aljic's house. On this second occasion, Milan Lukic was standing immediately beside the door of the Meho Aljic house. The same door that would later be barricaded as the last of the victims walked into the house. Milan Lukic was necessarily close enough to touch Ms. Turjacanin at this point. Ms. Turjacanin clearly had an excellent opportunity to observe Milan Lukic on this occasion. She also had an excellent basis to recognise him. She attended secondary school in Visegrad at the same school Milan Lukic attended. She was older than him and, consequently, was in her fourth year of secondary school when Milan Lukic was in his first. Ms. Turjacanin's brother, Dzevad Turjacanin, was younger than she was, and was in the same class as Milan Lukic. In fact, Ms. Turjacanin's brother Dzevad sat at the same school table as Milan Lukic. During their school days, Ms. Turjacanin saw Milan Lukic during breaks between classes at school. Students who smoked would go behind the school for a cigarette during these break times. Since both Ms. Turjacanin and Milan Lukic smoked, she would see him there behind the school during class breaks. In addition to this strong foundation of prior familiarity with Milan Lukic, Ms. Turjacanin also had three opportunities to observe him in person after his return to Visegrad in 1992, and before the night of the fire. The first of these opportunities arose in the afternoon of a day in June. Ms. Turjacanin was at the house of her neighbour. At one point, Milan Lukic arrived at the house, politely greeted the ladies, and told them that he would protect them. He stood about a metre away. She had a clear view of him in good light. She immediately recognised him as Milan Lukic. On another afternoon in June, Ms. Turjacanin saw Milan Lukic at her place of work in Visegrad, which was a lady's clothing factory. Milan Lukic had come to that factory to find one of his neighbours, a woman who also worked at the factory. Ms. Turjacanin's third opportunity to observe Milan Lukic occurred in late June 1992. On that occasion, she watched as group of soldiers brought by Milan Lukic burned two men to death. Milan Lukic and his group doused the two men with gasoline and set them on fire. In sum, Ms. Turjacanin knew who Milan Lukic was from their school days. She then saw him clearly on multiple occasions in June, and was in a good position to recognise him when she saw him on the 27th of June, shortly before the Bikavac fire. VG-035's contact with Milan Lukic began on the 26th of June. On that day, Milan Lukic appeared outside her house with a Serb boy. Milan Lukic introduced himself by name. She testified that when she learned who he was, she was frightened. She had heard that he had been doing bad things in Visegrad. Milan Lukic asked the witness about her husband, where she got her house, where she was working, and as they were discussing these matters, they also discussed their ages. And Milan Lukic told VG-035 that he was born in 1967. When VG-035 told Milan Lukic that she didn't know where her husband was, Milan Lukic said, "I'll check and I'll be back to tell you. If you are lying to me, I will kill you." During the course of this conversation, VG-035 and Milan Lukic were less than a metre away from each other. At the end of the conversation, Milan Lukic told her that he would return. Milan and Sredoje Lukic had been banging on the door of the house where VG-035 was staying with her family. When her mother-in-law answered the door, Milan and Sredoje Lukic barged into the house and entered the bedroom where VG-035 was lying in bed, and pulled the bed covers off. He was standing immediately beside her bed with nothing obstructing his face. Sredoje Lukic stood behind him. VG-035 recognised Milan Lukic as the person who had introduced himself to her in front of the house the day before. Milan Lukic returned several hours later, again banging on the door of the house. Again VG-035's mother-in-law opening the door. He took her out of the house and put her in the back seat of the car that had been owned by Ekrem Dzafic. He drove the two of them to a house owned by the Forta family in an area called Megdan. Your Honour, I'd ask that we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As discussed earlier, VG-035 saw Milan Lukic again around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon when he returned to her house. VG-035 thus had the opportunity to see and observe Milan Lukic in the closest possible proximity for several hours over the course of two days. There can be no doubt that the image of Milan Lukic was crystal clear and fresh in VG-035's mind on the day, when she recognised him again, of the Bikavac fire. VG-119 was also very familiar with Milan Lukic. She had recently had two opportunities to observe him at close range for extended periods of time. VG-119's first opportunity to observe Milan Lukic came in late May of 1992. Her and her family had attempted to flee from Visegrad to Belgrade, but were turned back in Priboj, Serbia. When they returned to Visegrad, the taxi that they were riding in was stopped at the old bridge in Visegrad by three cars filled with armed soldiers. One of the cars was the Zukic red Passat that VG-119 recognised. Four or five soldiers got out of these cars. One of them was Milan Lukic. Although VG-119 had not known Milan Lukic previously, her husband did and he identified him to her. Milan Lukic ordered VG-119's family to get back into the taxi and to go to their home in Dusce. Milan Lukic and the other soldiers got into their cars and followed the taxi to VG-119's home. When they reached their home, Milan Lukic ordered the women to go inside. He took VG-119's husband away in his car, while VG-119's father-in-law was taken away in another car. Neither was seen alive again. VG-119's second opportunity to observe Milan Lukic occurred later that same day, at about 8.00 in the evening. Milan Lukic arrived at her house and asked for the wife of the husband he had taken away earlier in the day. He took VG-119 and put her in the red Passat. He drove her to the Vilina Vlas Hotel where she remained for several hours. Later that night, a Serb soldier who she had seen earlier in the night reappeared and on Milan Lukic's instructions took VG-119 back home to Dusce. That night, VG-119 and the other women she was hiding with decided to leave Dusce because they were afraid Milan Lukic would return. They left the house in Dusce for Bikavac, where they were on the night of the Bikavac fire. Thus, prior to the night of the Bikavac fire, VG-119 had the opportunity to observe Milan Lukic at very close range for a relatively long period of time on two occasions. On the night of the Bikavac fire, she saw him twice in the house where she was staying. In sum, VG-119 had an excellent basis on which to identify Milan Lukic and an excellent opportunity to observe him in order to do so. These identifications were made by four witnesses who were very familiar with Milan Lukic before the night in question. These four identifications are also independent. None of the four witnesses' identifications is based on information received or related to any other witness. Indeed, none of the four witnesses were even in the same place at the time they saw Milan Lukic. Finally, the testimony of these four witnesses gives a very clear and consistent picture of the events of that night, indicating that these witnesses have strong, independent recollections of these events. In light of this evidence, the Prosecution submits that a reasonable trier of fact could clearly convict Milan Lukic of Counts 13 through 17 of the indictment. The murder of Hajra Koric. On a day between the 1st of July and the 5th of July, Hajra Koric was brutally murdered by Milan Lukic. VG-035, an eyewitness to the murder, stated: "Milan Lukic shot Hajra Koric. No one else." The Prosecution has led evidence from one eyewitness, VG-035, regarding the killing of Hajra Koric. As VG-035's ability to identify Milan Lukic on that day that Ms. Koric was killed is one of the key aspects of the Prosecution's case with respect to these counts, the basis of VG-035's familiarity with Milan Lukic has already been discussed in detail. Following the day of the Bikavac fire, the next time VG-035 saw Milan Lukic was on the day he killed Ms. Koric. At that time, VG-035 had moved to a house in the Potok neighbourhood of Visegrad, where a group of women and children were staying because this house was close to the bus station and VG-035 had been trying to escape from Visegrad. At some point on that day of Hajra Koric's murder, a group of soldiers entered the house where VG-035 was staying. Ms. Koric hid under the kitchen table, but the soldiers chased her and the other women and children out of the house. In the midst of the turmoil, Milan Lukic and his group appeared. After he stopped the group, Milan Lukic lined the women up. Ms. Koric was last in line. Milan Lukic and another man went from woman to woman looking for Hajra Koric. When Milan Lukic recognised her, he pulled her out of the line. After Milan Lukic questioned Ms. Koric, he shot her in the chest. He laughed as she fell to the ground, and said, "What is she doing?" Milan Lukic then turned Hajra Koric over with his foot and shot her once in the back. After this, she gave no signs of life. Your Honours, I will not address the evidence with respect to Uzamnica. Now having detailed the acts of the accused and summarized the relevant evidence, I will now turn my attention to the actual charges and the establishment of the required elements. As Judge Parker said in delivering the 98 bis decision in the Mrksic case on the 28th of June of 2006, "There must be evidence which meets the standard that we have set out above in respect of every element of the offence alleged by the count." The two broad categories of crimes alleged in the indictment are crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war. I will summarize the applicable law and incorporate by reference my earlier submissions on the evidence without repeating what I have said so far. I will first deal with crimes against humanity. What distinguishes ordinary crimes perpetrated during times of chaos and crimes against humanity is the connection these crimes have to a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population. This chapeau can be broken down into five constituent elements. The first element is the existence of an attack. An attack is distinguished from an armed conflict and is -- in its simplest terms, constitutes acts of violence perpetrated against a civilian population. It is not necessary to recount the six comprehensive factors enunciated by the Trial Chamber in the Dragan Nikolic Rule 61 decision. It is clear that what happened to the civilian population of Visegrad was very much an attack on its civilian Muslim population. The goal of the attack was the ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population of Visegrad. The second chapeau element is the connection between the attack on the civilian population and the acts of the accused as required or as defined in the Vasiljevic trial judgement at paragraph 32 and the Kunarac trial judgement at 418, which set out two factors for consideration. First, did the conduct of the accused, by its nature and effect, further the attack on the civilian population? Second, was the accused aware that his acts were part of an overall attack? In the context of this case, both are abundantly clear. The selection of victims, the timing of the crimes, the pattern of searching for men and then killing large numbers of women, elderly and children, all lead to the inescapable conclusion that the acts of Milan and Sredoje Lukic was in fact, and in their minds, inextricably connected to the overall campaign of ethnic cleansing of Muslims in Bosnia during the spring and summer of 1992. The third element require that is the attack be directed at the civilian population. In other words, that it be the target of the attack. Again would I cite the Kunarac Appeals Chamber judgement, this time at paragraph 91. In this case there can be no doubt that the careful selection of civilians, the inducements offered a fearful and terrified people made clear that it was the civilians of Visegrad that the attack was directed against. The fourth element, the widespread or systematic nature of the attack, this element defines a crime against humanity, not only by its target, but also by its scale. Was it widespread or systematic? Widespread connotes the scale of the crimes, and in this case you have heard compelling demographic and pathology evidence indicating the widespread nature of the crimes perpetrated against the civilian population in Visegrad. With respect to systematic, this refers to the organisation of the attack. Were the crimes a disconnected series of events that simply coincided with each other? Or, as required by crimes against humanity, were they the result of a organised effort? In addition to the demographic evidence, the Chamber has heard sufficient evidence to conclude that the attack on the civilian population of Visegrad proceeded by way of a system ensuring the destruction of the Muslim population. Targeting entire villages such as Koritnik and Bikavac, going house to house for an intense and unrelenting period of ethnic cleansing. The fifth element concerns the mens rea of the accused, and the Prosecution must establish that the accused is aware that there is an attack on the civilian population, and that his acts are part of or are connected to the attack. This was first enunciated in the Blaskic Appeals Chamber judgement at paragraphs 124 to 127. The record is replete with evidence from which a reasonable Trial Chamber could find that both of these accused acted with full knowledge that their conduct was not only part of the attack on the civilian population of Visegrad, but was in fact the primary attack on the civilian population itself. Count 1 of the indictment charges the first crime against humanity, the crime of persecution. Persecution on political, racial or religious grounds is a crime against humanity that, in addition to the chapeau elements, has three underlying elements. One, the occurrence of a discriminatory act or omission. Two, the discriminatory basis was on political, religious or racial grounds. And three, the accused intended to cause and, in fact, did cause an infringement of an individual's enjoyment of a fundamental right. While persecutory acts can encompass a plethora of serious infringements on personal rights, for the purposes of this indictment against both accused, the Prosecution's case, as set out in the second amended indictment, alleges five such persecutory acts. In paragraphs 4(a), 4(c), 4(d), and 4(e), the Prosecution alleges Milan and Sredoje Lukic's treatment and conduct towards approximately 140 Muslim civilians constitutes persecutory acts. These acts included their confinement, the theft of their personal property, their harassment, humiliation and psychological abuse, as well as their subsequent murder by setting them on fire. With respect to Milan Lukic alone, the Prosecution also asserts in paragraphs 4(a) and 4(d), that his treatment and murder of Muslims at the Drina on June 7th, the Varda factory on June 10th, and Hajrija Koric also constitutes persecutory acts. In paragraph 4(b), the Prosecution has established that the cruel and inhumane treatment of the Muslim detainees at the Uzamnica camp were also persecutory acts. I've already summarized the evidence of all of these acts and will not recall it again, other than to remind the Chamber that all of the victims in this case were Muslims, and during the course of the crimes, many of the witnesses refer to derogatory language used to refer to them as Muslims, words such as "balija." The evidence is ample and compelling and clearly meets the test set forth by Rule 98 bis. Murder as a crime against humanity has been charged in Count 2 with respect to the Drina River incident, Count 6 related to the Varda factory killings, Count 9 related to Pionirska Street fire, Count 14 related to the fire in Bikavac, and Count 18 related to the killing of Ms. Koric. The elements of murder as a crime against humanity, and murder as a violation -- I should say the underlying elements of murder as a crime against humanity and murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war are essentially the same except for their chapeau elements. The elements of murder are the death of the victim, the death was caused by an act of the accused, and thirdly, the act was done with the intention to kill or to inflict grievous bodily harm in the reasonable knowledge that such was likely to cause death. In the case of every criminal event alleged in the indictment, it has been clearly established that the deaths of the victim were the product of the intentional conduct of these two accused. The victims were either shot to death or burned to death. Inhumane acts as a crime against humanity has been charged in Count 4 with respect to the Drina River incident, Count 11 related to Pionirska Street fire, Count 16 related to the Bikavac fire, and Count 20 related to the Uzamnica camp. The concept of inhumane acts is a broad one and of a residual nature, in that it casts a large net to encompass criminal acts not specifically enumerated in other specific crimes against humanity. The elements may be listed as: One, it is an act of like seriousness to other enumerated acts under Article 5. The act caused serious mental or physical suffering or injury, and constituted a serious attack on human dignity. And lastly, the attack was performed intentionally by the accused. The evidence clearly establishes that each of the accused -- and this clearly establishes that each accused, in the counts on which they have been charged, have committed the crime of inhumane acts with respect to the survivors of those crimes. Extermination as a crime against humanity has been charged in Counts 8 and 13 with respect to fires in Pionirska Street and Bikavac, respectively. Quoting from the Akayesu trial judgement at paragraph 591: "Extermination is a crime which by its very nature is directed against a group of individuals. Extermination differs from murder in that it requires an element of mass destruction which is not required for murder." There is no minimum threshold or number of victims. With respect to the mens rea, the Prosecution must establish that the person intended to kill a large number of individuals or to intentionally inflict grievous bodily harm to a large number of people with the knowledge that such was likely to cause death. The Prosecutor must not only prove that the perpetrator intended to kill the individual victim with knowledge of the larger murderous context, I'm quoting from Mr. Mettraux's book, International Crimes and the Ad Hoc Tribunals, at page 179. As the Ruzindana Trial Chamber stated: "A single killing or a small number of killings do not constitute an extermination. In order to give practical meaning to the charge as distinct from murder, there must in fact be a large number of killings." The Prosecution has established with evidence upon which a reasonable Trial Chamber could convict Milan and Sredoje Lukic of extermination for their conduct as described in Counts 8 related to Pionirska Street, and Count 13 related to the Bikavac fires. Violations of the laws and customs of war. I now turn my attention to the violations of the laws and customs of war and begin by summarising the chapeau elements. In order for a crime to be considered a war crime it must be established first, that a state of armed conflict exists. And two, there is a nexus between the crime and the armed conflict. The Tadic jurisdictional decision was the first to deal with whether an armed conflict existed in Bosnia, and in determining that it did, it found that when there is a "protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups, or between such groups within a state." That's paragraph 7, and a similar statement was made in the Kunarac appeals judgement at paragraph 56. There is no clear line or threshold indicating the level at which hostilities are sufficiently intense to constitute an armed conflict. The Trial Chambers have relied on a number of factors articulated in the Tadic trial judgement, the Akayesu Trial Chamber, and the Tadic jurisdictional decision, as well as several other significant judgements and decisions. The factors some of the factors that have been relied on include: One, the involvement of a large amount of weaponry and troops. Two, sustained and coordinated military operations. Three, inability of a state, in this case Bosnia, to control all of its territory. And four, the scope of the geographic area implicated in the conflict. Pictet, in the commentary on the Geneva Conventions says that the closely related criteria of intensity and organisation are used primarily "for the purpose as a minimum of distinguishing an armed conflict from banditry, unorganized and short-lived insurrections or terrorist activities which are not subject to international humanitarian law." That's page 33. The Tadic jurisdiction decision at paragraph 69 and 70 and the Kunarac appeals judgement at 57 and 64 hold that once established -- once it has been established that an armed conflict is in existence, the laws of war will in principle apply and continue to apply until a general conclusion of peace or until a peaceful settlement has been reached. That clearly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, in the Slobodan Milosevic case, the Trial Chamber wrote a Rule 98 bis decision which was 187 pages, I think. Are you threatening to challenge that length? I hope not. It was shortly after that that the present Rule 98 bis was formulated by the plenary, and I wonder whether we need all the detail that you are offering us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be guided by the Chamber. I took some of the comments from before the break that this was a primary area of concern for the Chamber. I will move from -- I don't mean to insult the Chamber by citing so much of the law, so let me move to some of the evidence that the Chamber has heard on this issue. In this case, VG-011 testified: "In April 1992, that is to say the beginning of April, barricades were set up, set up by both sides. A paramilitary unit from Serbia was introduced into the Dobrun territory and there was an armed conflict. According to the documents that were seized by one such group, the people involved were so-called White Eagles." That was from the witness's testimony in Vasiljevic on the 12th of September, 2001. Mirsada Kahriman who testified before you, stated: "The war in the area started around 5th of April, 1992, when the area was shelled from the direction of the Serbian border." VG-025, in his 92 quater statement that is now in evidence as P168: "After this we started to organise ourselves into some sort of Territorial Defence which developed into some sort of army. We were considered as members of the BiH Army from the 11th of June, 1992." There's a statement of Milan Lukic in evidence, a statement that was given to a witness of Serb -- someone from the Serb government and it's Prosecution Exhibit 149. Quoting from that, this is Milan Lukic's own words: "I have been on the front in Visegrad and its surroundings since the 10th of April, 1992. I am the commander of a group called the Avengers. The group has between 20 and 50 men and is under the command of the Visegrad TO." So Your Honours, I believe -- well, let me make mention of one more, it's an adjudicated fact. Fact number 10 that the Chamber found to be an adjudicated fact was that the Uzice Corps entered Visegrad on the 14th of April. So Your Honours, I believe there is ample evidence that an armed conflict was in existence prior to the commission of any of the crimes in the indictment, and there certainly is no evidence that there was a general cessation of hostilities during the period of the indictment. Murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war has been charged in Count 3 with respect to the Drina River incident, Count 7 related to the Varda factory killings, Count 10 related to Pionirska Street fire, Count 15 related to the fire in Bikavac, and Count 19 related to the killing of Ms. Koric. As I've said earlier, the underlying elements are essentially the same for whether the crime is charged as a crime against humanity or violation of the laws or customs of war. I incorporate these elements and my comments about the evidence into this part of my argument. Cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war has been charged in Count 5 with respect to the Drina River incident, Count 12 related to Pionirska Street, Count 17 related to Bikavac, and Count 21 related to Uzamnica. The Celebici Trial Chamber, in paragraph 50 of its judgement, characterized cruel treatment as "treatment that is inhumane." Cruel treatment, inhumane treatment and inhumane acts essentially require similar proof. The elements can be defined as an intentional act which causes serious mental or physical suffering, or constitutes a serious attack on a person's dignity. The attack is perpetrated against someone who is not participating in the hostilities, and the mens rea element is that the perpetrator of the cruel treatment did so intentionally. Once again, the charge of cruel treatment as it relates to each accused has been clearly established by the survivors of the crimes that have been charged. Your Honours, that concludes my submission on the Rule 98 bis. The Prosecution in its case in chief has adduced ample and compelling evidence upon which a reasonable Trial Chamber could enter a conviction on the charges contained in the indictment against Milan and Sredoje Lukic. I thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Any reply, Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, and I guess I'm slightly more baited into the -- into a couple of issues on the facts and one would be, like, 115, VG-115 who supposedly witnessed Bikavac. Well, if you put Ms. Turjacanin's and 115's maps of the neighbourhood together, then VG-115 is in the orchard with the soldiers who are out of ammo and drugged up and letting Ms. Turjacanin walk by. Just by virtue of the way the maps rode out. So, you know, those are one of the things where I think the inconsistencies or the differences between two statements create an illogical premise. Going back, though, to, I think, the more legal side of it which is whether or not -- I do find it hard that Mr. Groome relies on lay witnesses to establish the existence of the armed conflict in compliance with the statute. I understand perceptions might think of it that way. However, I don't believe these perceptions would rise to the level of a legal conclusion which would satisfy the jurisdiction of the Court. If you take into consideration that no banditry or terrorism is not or does not fall into the jurisprudence and jurisdiction of an international Tribunal, that is the nature of the argument, because at this stage -- and I would also take exception to characterizing the summary of Mr. Lukic's supported supposed interrogation as a statement. Regardless of what Mr. Lukic says, he even cannot establish the existence of an armed conflict despite the fact that -- that those words in a summary are trying to be used against him for purposes of establishing that. I think at the very worst case scenario, assuming all facts in favour of the Prosecution, they still have not established that this was not simply banditry or terrorism, which would fall outside the scope of jurisdiction of the Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I thank all the parties for their submissions. The Trial Chamber will consider them carefully and give its decision tomorrow. We are adjourned.
